exercises.title: Rotate a list to the right
exercises.prompt:
Write `rotate_right(nums, k)` that returns a **new** list with the elements of `nums` rotated `k` positions to the right.

- `k` can be larger than the length of the list.
- An empty list returns `[]`.
- Do not modify `nums`.

Example: `rotate_right([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)` returns `[4, 5, 1, 2, 3]`.
exercises.starter:
def rotate_right(nums, k):
    pass
hints: `nums[-k:]` is the last k elements, `nums[:-k]` is everything before them.
Reduce k first with `k % len(nums)` (guard against an empty list).
exercises.explanation: Slicing always builds a new list, so `nums[-k:] + nums[:-k]` rotates without touching the input. Reducing `k` with `%` handles rotations bigger than the list. A common pitfall: `len(nums)` is 0 for an empty list, so `k % 0` raises ZeroDivisionError unless you return early.

review.why: A negative start counts from the end.
A negative step walks backwards from the end.

review.q: What does `b = a[:]` give you?
review.why: A full slice builds a new list, but nested objects are still shared (shallow).

review.code: last_three = nums[____]
review.why: Start 3 from the end, go to the end.

more.prompt:
Write `rotate_left(nums, k)` that returns a **new** list with the elements of `nums` rotated `k` positions to the **left** (the first items move to the end).

- `k` can be larger than the length of the list.
- An empty list returns `[]`.
- Do not modify `nums`.

Example: `rotate_left([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)` returns `[3, 4, 5, 1, 2]`.

**At work:** you re-order a list of weekly figures so the series starts on another week.
hints: `nums[k:]` is everything after the first k items, `nums[:k]` is the first k items.
Reduce k first with `k % len(nums)`, after checking the list is not empty.
more.explanation: Rotating left is the mirror of rotating right: the first `k` items go to the end, so `nums[k:] + nums[:k]`. Slices build a new list, so the input stays untouched.

more.prompt:
An on-call rota lists the team's days. Write `shift_rota(days, k)` that returns a **new** list rotated `k` positions to the **right** (the last days move to the front).

- `k` can be larger than the length of the list.
- An empty list returns `[]`.
- Do not modify `days`.

Example: `shift_rota(['Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri'], 1)` returns `['Fri', 'Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu']`.
hints: `days[-k:]` is the last k days, `days[:-k]` is everything before them.
Reduce k first with `k % len(days)`, after checking the list is not empty.
more.explanation: It is the same slice trick as `rotate_right`, on strings instead of numbers: slicing does not care what is in the list.

more.prompt:
Your client's fiscal year does not start in January. Write `fiscal_order(months, k)` that returns a **new** list rotated `k` positions to the **left**, so the list starts at month number `k`.

- `k` can be larger than the length of the list.
- An empty list returns `[]`.
- Do not modify `months`.

Example: `fiscal_order(['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar', 'Apr', 'May', 'Jun'], 3)` returns `['Apr', 'May', 'Jun', 'Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar']`.
hints: A left rotation is `months[k:] + months[:k]`.
Guard the empty list before `k % len(months)`.
more.explanation: Two slices glued together rotate the list without a loop, and `%` brings any `k` back into range. Always guard the empty list, because `k % 0` raises an error.

exercises.title: Split a list into chunks
exercises.prompt:
Write `chunk(items, size)` that splits `items` into consecutive lists of length `size` (the last one may be shorter). Assume `size >= 1`.

Example: `chunk([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2)` returns `[[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]`.
exercises.starter:
def chunk(items, size):
    pass
hints: `range(0, len(items), size)` gives the start index of each chunk.
Slicing past the end is safe: `[1, 2][0:10]` is `[1, 2]`.
exercises.explanation: A comprehension over `range(start, stop, step)` produces each chunk's start index, and slicing does the rest. Slices never raise for out-of-range bounds, which is why the short last chunk needs no special case. Pitfall: a `while` loop with manual index updates is easy to get off by one.

review.code: print(list(range(0, 7, 3)))
review.why: Start at 0, step 3, stop before 7.

review.code: print([x for row in [[1, 2], [3]] for x in row])
review.why: Nested for clauses read left to right, like nested loops: this flattens.

review.q: What does `list(zip(*[[1, 2], [3, 4]]))` return?
review.why: `zip(*rows)` transposes: it pairs the first items, then the second items.

more.prompt:
Your mailing tool accepts at most `size` addresses per send. Write `batches(emails, size)` that splits `emails` into consecutive lists of length `size` (the last one may be shorter). Assume `size >= 1`.

Example: `batches(['a@x.com', 'b@x.com', 'c@x.com'], 2)` returns `[['a@x.com', 'b@x.com'], ['c@x.com']]`.
hints: `range(0, len(emails), size)` gives the start index of each batch.
Slicing past the end is safe: `['a'][0:5]` is `['a']`.
more.explanation: The comprehension walks over start positions 0, size, 2*size... and slices one batch at a time. Slices never fail past the end, so the short last batch needs no special case.

more.prompt:
A report shows `per_page` rows per page. Write `pages(rows, per_page)` that splits `rows` into consecutive pages (the last page may be shorter). Assume `per_page >= 1`.

Example: `pages([101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 107], 3)` returns `[[101, 102, 103], [104, 105, 106], [107]]`.
hints: The start of each page is 0, per_page, 2 * per_page... which is `range(0, len(rows), per_page)`.
One page is `rows[i:i + per_page]`.
more.explanation: Same pattern as chunking: start indexes from `range` with a step, and a slice for each page. This is how APIs and dashboards paginate results.

more.prompt:
You seat workshop attendees at tables of `size` people. Write `tables(names, size)` that splits `names` into consecutive groups of `size` (the last table may have fewer people). Assume `size >= 1`.

Example: `tables(['Ana', 'Bo', 'Cy', 'Dee', 'Ed'], 2)` returns `[['Ana', 'Bo'], ['Cy', 'Dee'], ['Ed']]`.
hints: Loop over start positions with `range(0, len(names), size)`.
Take `names[i:i + size]` at each start.
more.explanation: A comprehension over `range(start, stop, step)` gives each group's start, and the slice does the rest, even for the short last group.

exercises.title: Five most expensive products
exercises.prompt:
From `products`, return `product_id`, `name`, `price` for the **5 most expensive** products.

Sort by `price` descending, then by `name` ascending to break ties (two products cost 1299).
exercises.starter:
SELECT 
FROM products
hints: `ORDER BY price DESC, name ASC` sorts by the second key only within equal prices.
`LIMIT 5` goes at the very end of the query.
exercises.explanation: ORDER BY accepts several keys; the second one only matters when the first is tied. Without a tie-breaker, the order of tied rows is not guaranteed, so `LIMIT` can return different rows from one run (or one database) to the next. Always add a deterministic tie-breaker before a LIMIT.

review.q: In which order does SQL logically evaluate these clauses?
options: FROM, WHERE, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT
review.why: FROM/WHERE build the rows, SELECT shapes them, ORDER BY sorts, LIMIT cuts.

review.code:
SELECT name, price FROM products
ORDER BY price ____, name
LIMIT 3
review.why: Most expensive first means descending price.

review.front: Why add a tie-breaker column before LIMIT?
review.back: Rows with equal sort keys come back in arbitrary order, so the top-N would not be deterministic.

more.prompt:

Sort by `salary` descending, then by `name` ascending.
hints: `ORDER BY salary DESC` puts the biggest first.
`LIMIT 5` keeps the first 5 rows.
more.explanation: Sort, then cut with LIMIT. A NULL salary sorts last when you sort descending in SQLite.

exercises.title: Countries we sell to
exercises.prompt: Return a single column `country`: each country present in `customers`, **once**, excluding missing (NULL) countries. Sort alphabetically.
exercises.starter:
SELECT country
FROM customers
hints: `SELECT DISTINCT col` removes duplicate values.
`country != NULL` is never true: use `IS NOT NULL`.
exercises.explanation: DISTINCT deduplicates the whole selected row, here just one column. NULL is not a value but 'unknown', so comparisons like `= NULL` or `<> NULL` return NULL (treated as false) and filter out everything. The only correct tests are `IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL`.

review.q: What does `WHERE country = NULL` return?
review.why: Any comparison with NULL yields NULL, which WHERE treats as false.

review.code:
SELECT DISTINCT country FROM customers
WHERE country IS ____ NULL
review.why: IS NOT NULL keeps known values.

review.front: `SELECT DISTINCT a, b` deduplicates what exactly?
review.back: Whole (a, b) combinations, not each column separately.

review.code:
import sqlite3
c = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
print(c.execute("SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT x) FROM (SELECT 'a' AS x UNION ALL SELECT 'a' UNION ALL SELECT NULL UNION ALL SELECT 'b')").fetchone()[0])
review.why: COUNT(DISTINCT x) ignores NULL: only 'a' and 'b' are counted.

more.prompt: Return a single column `segment`: each customer segment in `customers`, **once**, excluding missing (NULL) segments. Sort alphabetically.
hints: `SELECT DISTINCT` removes repeats.
Use `IS NOT NULL`, not `!= NULL`.
more.explanation: DISTINCT keeps one row per value; the WHERE drops the NULL segment.

more.prompt: Return a single column `department`: each department in `employees`, **once**, excluding missing (NULL) departments. Sort alphabetically.
hints: `SELECT DISTINCT department`.
Filter with `WHERE department IS NOT NULL`.
more.explanation: Five departments remain once repeats and the NULL are removed.

more.prompt: Return a single column `device`: each device seen in `web_events`, **once**, excluding missing (NULL) devices. Sort alphabetically.
hints: `SELECT DISTINCT device`.
`IS NOT NULL` removes the missing ones.
more.explanation: Desktop, mobile and tablet: DISTINCT collapses 51 rows into 3 values.

exercises.title: Most frequent words
exercises.prompt:
Write `top_words(text, n)` returning the `n` most frequent words as a list of `(word, count)` tuples.

- Lowercase the text and split on whitespace.
- Strip the punctuation characters `.,!?;:` from both ends of each word; ignore words that become empty.
- Sort by count descending, then alphabetically for ties.

Example: `top_words("the cat and the hat. The end!", 2)` returns `[("the", 3), ("and", 1)]`.
exercises.starter:
def top_words(text, n):
    pass
hints: `collections.Counter` counts an iterable in one line.
`most_common` does not break ties alphabetically; sort `counts.items()` yourself.
Key for 'count desc, word asc': `lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0])`.
exercises.explanation: Counter turns counting into one line, and sorting with a tuple key gives a multi-level order. Negating the count makes it descending while the word stays ascending. Pitfall: `Counter.most_common(n)` keeps insertion order for ties, which is not alphabetical.

review.code:
from collections import Counter
print(Counter('abca').most_common(1))
review.why: most_common returns (item, count) tuples, largest first.

review.q: `c = Counter('ab')`. What is `c['z']`?
review.why: A Counter returns 0 for missing keys instead of raising.

review.front: How do you sort by count descending, then name ascending?
review.back: `sorted(items, key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0]))`: a tuple key, with the number negated.

review.code: counts = Counter(w ____ w in words)
review.why: Counter accepts a generator expression.

Sort `counts.items()` with `key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0])`.
more.explanation: Clean, count, sort: the same three steps as `top_words`. The tuple key sorts by count (negated, so descending) and then by name for ties.

more.prompt:

`Counter` counts, then sort with `(-count, code)`.

Write `invert(d)` that maps each **value** of `d` to the **sorted list of keys** that have that value. Return a plain dict.

Example: `invert({"ana": "Paris", "bo": "Lyon", "cy": "Paris"})` returns `{"Paris": ["ana", "cy"], "Lyon": ["bo"]}`.

    pass
hints: `defaultdict(list)` creates an empty list the first time you touch a key.
Sort each list at the end with a dict comprehension.
exercises.explanation: `defaultdict(list)` removes the 'is the key there yet?' check when grouping. Values become keys, so they must be hashable (strings, numbers, tuples; not lists). Pitfall: `dict.setdefault(k, []).append(x)` works too, but it builds a throwaway list on every call.

review.why: `&` is set intersection.

review.q: Which expression gives the items in `a` that are not in `b` (both sets)?
review.why: `-` is difference; `^` is symmetric difference (in exactly one of them).

review.code:
from collections import defaultdict
counts = defaultdict(____)
counts['x'] += 1
review.why: `int()` returns 0, a handy default for counters.

review.code:
d = {'a': 1}
print(d.get('b', 0), len(d))
review.why: `get` returns the default without inserting the key.

exercises.title: Clean a list of words
exercises.prompt:
Write `clean_words(text, stopwords)` that returns the words of `text` **in lowercase**, in their original order, **without** the words that are in `stopwords`.

Example: `clean_words("The cat THE hat", {"the"})` returns `["cat", "hat"]`.

**At work:** you count the words in 2,000 customer reviews. "the", "a" and "and" always come out on top and tell the client nothing. Removing them first puts "late", "broken" and "refund" at the top of your chart. Lowercasing first makes "Delivery" and "DELIVERY" count as the same word.

Build it in this order:
1. an empty box: `words = []`
2. loop over the **words**, not the letters: `for word in text.split():`
3. lowercase the current word
4. if it is not a stopword, `append` it to the box
5. `return` the box, **after** the loop (not indented under the `for`)
exercises.starter:
def clean_words(text, stopwords):
    words = []
    # your loop here
    return words
hints: `text.split()` gives a list of words. Looping over `text` directly gives letters.
Lowercase BEFORE checking: `word = word.lower()`, then `if word not in stopwords:`.
`return words` must line up with `for`, not sit inside it, or the function stops after the first word.
exercises.explanation: The pattern is: empty box, loop, `append`, then return after the loop. `word` holds one word at a time and is replaced on every pass, while `words` grows. Lowercasing before the `in` check matters: `'The' in {'the'}` is False. The one-line version is `[w.lower() for w in text.split() if w.lower() not in stopwords]`.

review.code:
for t in 'hi':
    print(t)
review.why: Looping over a string gives one character at a time, not words.

review.q: `words = []` then `for w in text.split(): words.append(w)`. What is `w`?
options: One word, a new one on each pass
review.why: The loop puts the next word in `w` on every pass; `words` is the result box.
`split()` cuts the text into words at the spaces.

review.front: Why lowercase before checking `if word not in stopwords`?
review.back: Because `'The' in {'the'}` is False: without lowercasing, capitalised stopwords slip through.

Write `build_url(base, *path, **params)` that returns a web address as a string.

- Each item of `path` is added after `base` with a `/` in front.
- Each param becomes `name=value` (use `str()`), joined with `&` after a `?`, in the order given. Params whose value is `None` are skipped.
- No params left means no `?`.

Examples:
- `build_url("https://api.shop.com")` returns `"https://api.shop.com"`
- `build_url("https://api.shop.com", "orders", status="paid", page=2)` returns `"https://api.shop.com/orders?status=paid&page=2"`

**At work:** you call a client's API page by page to download their data.
hints: `path` is a tuple and `params` is a dict, both in call order.
Build the list of `name=value` pieces first, then add `?` only if it is not empty.
more.explanation: `*path` collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and `**params` collects keyword arguments into a dict. Real code would use `urllib.parse.urlencode`, which also escapes special characters.

more.prompt:
Write `log_line(level, *tags, **fields)` that returns one line of a log as a string.

- It starts with the level in brackets: `[INFO]`.
- Then each tag, then each field as `name=value`, in the order given. String values are wrapped in single quotes; other values use `str()`.
- All pieces are separated by one space.

Examples:
- `log_line("INFO")` returns `"[INFO]"`
- `log_line("INFO", "api", user="ana", ms=120)` returns `"[INFO] api user='ana' ms=120"`

**At work:** clear log lines make a failed nightly data job easy to debug.
hints: Start a list with `f'[{level}]'`, add the tags, then one piece per field.
`isinstance(v, str)` tells you when to add quotes; `' '.join(parts)` glues the pieces.
more.explanation: `*tags` arrives as a tuple and `**fields` as a dict that keeps the call order. Building a list of pieces and joining it once is cleaner than adding spaces by hand.

more.prompt:
Write `count_query(table, *group_cols, **filters)` that returns a SQL string that counts rows.

- With no group columns: `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM table`.
- With group columns: `SELECT col1, col2, COUNT(*) FROM table ... GROUP BY col1, col2`.
- Each filter becomes `name = value`, joined with `" AND "` after `WHERE` (before `GROUP BY`), in the order given. String values are wrapped in single quotes; other values use `str()`.

Examples:
- `count_query("orders")` returns `"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders"`
- `count_query("orders", "region", status="paid")` returns `"SELECT region, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY region"`
hints: `group_cols` is a tuple: `', '.join(group_cols)` makes the column list.
Add the WHERE part first, then the GROUP BY part, each only when needed.
more.explanation: The same `*args` / `**kwargs` pattern as `build_query`, with one more optional piece. In real code, pass values as query parameters to avoid SQL injection.

exercises.title: Customers who never ordered
exercises.prompt:
Find customers with **no row at all** in `orders`.

Return `customer_id`, `name`, `signup_date`. Sort by `customer_id`.
exercises.starter:
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, c.signup_date
FROM customers c
hints: Pattern: LEFT JOIN, then keep rows where the right side's key IS NULL.
Alternative: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)`.
exercises.explanation: An anti-join returns left rows without a match. `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.key IS NULL` and `NOT EXISTS` are the two safe idioms. `NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM ...)` is risky: if the subquery returns a single NULL, `NOT IN` returns no rows at all.

review.q: `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT x FROM t)` and t.x contains a NULL. Result?
review.why: `id <> NULL` is unknown, so NOT IN can never be true.

review.code:
SELECT c.* FROM customers c
WHERE ____ EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id)
review.why: NOT EXISTS is the NULL-safe anti-join.

review.front: Anti-join with LEFT JOIN: which column do you test for NULL?
review.back: A NOT NULL column of the right table, typically its primary/join key.

exercises.title: An invoice line as a dataclass
exercises.prompt:
Define a dataclass `Item` with fields `name: str`, `price: float` and `qty: int = 1`.

- Add a method `total()` returning `price * qty`.
- Raise `ValueError` when `price` is negative (use `__post_init__`).

Example: `Item("pen", 2.5, 4).total()` returns `10.0`, and `Item("pen", 2.5)` has `qty == 1`.
hints: Fields are class-level annotations: `name: str`. Defaults go last.
`__post_init__(self)` runs right after the generated `__init__`.
exercises.explanation: `@dataclass` writes `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` for you from the annotated fields. Validation goes in `__post_init__`, which runs after the fields are set. Pitfall: a mutable default such as `tags: list = []` is rejected; use `field(default_factory=list)`.

review.front: Which methods does `@dataclass` generate by default?
review.back: `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` (add `order=True` for comparisons, `frozen=True` for immutability).

review.why: The generated repr lists every field.

review.q: How do you give a dataclass field an empty list as default?
review.why: default_factory builds a fresh list for each instance.

Example: `Order("Acme", 4.0, 3).total()` returns `12.0`, and `Order("Acme", 4.0)` has `qty == 1`.
hints: List the fields with annotations: `customer: str`. The field with a default goes last.
`__post_init__(self)` runs right after the generated `__init__`: check `self.qty` there.
more.explanation: `@dataclass` writes `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` from the fields. `__post_init__` is the place to reject bad data as soon as an object is created.

hints: Fields: `name: str`, `monthly_salary: float`, `months: int = 12`.
In `__post_init__`, `raise ValueError(...)` if `self.monthly_salary < 0`.
more.explanation: A dataclass is a tidy record: fields, defaults, a small method, and a check in `__post_init__`.

`def __post_init__(self):` then `if self.nightly_rate < 0: raise ValueError(...)`.

exercises.title: A Money class with dunder methods
exercises.prompt:
Write a class `Money(amount, currency="EUR")` with attributes `amount` and `currency`, and these behaviours:

- `Money(1) + Money(2) == Money(3)`. Adding two different currencies raises `ValueError`.
- `sum([Money(1), Money(2.5)])` works (hint: `sum` starts from `0`).
- `==` compares amount and currency; `<` compares amounts (same currency).
- `repr(Money(10.5))` returns `"Money(10.50, 'EUR')"` (2 decimals).
hints: `a + b` calls `a.__add__(b)`; `sum` starts with `0 + first`, which calls `first.__radd__(0)`.
In `__radd__`, return `self` when `other == 0`.
Format with `f"Money({self.amount:.2f}, '{self.currency}')"`.
exercises.explanation: Operators are method calls: `+` is `__add__`, `==` is `__eq__`, `<` is `__lt__`, and `repr()` is `__repr__`. `sum` begins with the integer 0, so `__radd__` must accept 0. Pitfall: defining `__eq__` sets `__hash__` to None, so instances can no longer go in a set or be dict keys unless you also define `__hash__`.

review.front: `__repr__` vs `__str__`?
review.back: `__repr__` is the unambiguous developer view (shown in the REPL and in containers); `__str__` is for print(). Without `__str__`, print uses `__repr__`.

review.why: len(obj) calls obj.__len__().

review.q: A class defines `__eq__` but not `__hash__`. What happens with `{obj}`?
review.why: Defining __eq__ sets __hash__ to None.

review.code:
def ____(self, other):   # called by a + b
    ...
review.why: The + operator dispatches to __add__.

more.prompt:
Write a class `Quantity(value, unit="kg")` with attributes `value` and `unit`, and these behaviours:

- `Quantity(1) + Quantity(2) == Quantity(3)`. Adding two different units raises `ValueError`.
- `sum([Quantity(1), Quantity(2.5)])` works (hint: `sum` starts from `0`).
- `==` compares value and unit; `<` compares values (same unit).
- `repr(Quantity(2.5))` returns `"Quantity(2.50, 'kg')"` (2 decimals).

**At work:** adding up shipped weights without mixing kg and lb.
hints: `a + b` calls `a.__add__(b)`; `sum` starts with `0 + first`, which calls `first.__radd__(0)`.
In `__radd__`, return `self` when `other == 0`.
Format with `f"Quantity({self.value:.2f}, '{self.unit}')"`.
more.explanation: Same design as `Money`: operators are methods (`__add__`, `__eq__`, `__lt__`, `__repr__`), and `__radd__` lets `sum` start from 0.

- `==` compares amount and team; `<` compares amounts (same team).
- `repr(Budget(1000))` returns `"Budget(1000.00, 'Sales')"` (2 decimals).

**At work:** totalling a client's budget lines without mixing departments.
hints: `__add__` checks the team, then returns a new `Budget`.
`sum` begins with `0 + first`: `__radd__` must return `self` when `other == 0`.
`__repr__` uses `{self.amount:.2f}`.
more.explanation: Defining the dunder methods makes your object work with `+`, `sum`, `==` and `<` like a number, while refusing to mix teams.

more.prompt:
Write a class `Hours(amount, project="ACME")` with attributes `amount` and `project`, and these behaviours:

- `sum([Hours(1), Hours(0.5)])` works (hint: `sum` starts from `0`).
- `==` compares amount and project; `<` compares amounts (same project).
- `repr(Hours(7.5))` returns `"Hours(7.50, 'ACME')"` (2 decimals).

**At work:** a consultant's timesheet, where hours are billed per project.
hints: `a + b` calls `a.__add__(b)`; raise `ValueError` when the projects differ.
`sum` starts with 0, so `__radd__` returns `self` when `other == 0`.
more.explanation: Operators are just method calls. Once `__add__` and `__radd__` exist, `sum(timesheet)` works on your own objects.

exercises.title: Price tiers
exercises.prompt:
Classify every product into a `price_tier`: `'budget'` if price < 50, `'mid'` if price < 300, otherwise `'premium'`.

Return `price_tier`, `n_products`, `avg_price` (`ROUND(AVG(price), 2)`). Sort by `avg_price` ascending.
exercises.starter:
SELECT price
FROM products
hints: CASE branches are tested top to bottom; the first true one wins.
SQLite lets you GROUP BY the alias `price_tier` (otherwise repeat the CASE).
exercises.explanation: CASE returns the first branch whose condition is true, so `WHEN price < 300` already implies `price >= 50`. Getting the branch order wrong (testing `< 300` first) puts every cheap product in 'mid'. Forgetting ELSE yields NULL for unmatched rows.

review.q: A CASE with no ELSE and no matching WHEN returns...
review.why: The implicit ELSE is NULL.

review.code:
CASE WHEN price < 50 THEN 'budget'
     ____ 'other' END
review.why: ELSE catches everything else.

review.code:
import sqlite3
c = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
print(c.execute("SELECT CASE WHEN 40 < 300 THEN 'mid' WHEN 40 < 50 THEN 'budget' END").fetchone()[0])
review.why: First true branch wins, so the order of WHENs matters.

exercises.title: Cancellation rate by segment
exercises.prompt:
For each customer `segment` (NULL segment included), compute over **all** orders:
- `n_orders`
- `n_cancelled` = orders with status `'cancelled'`
- `cancel_pct` = `ROUND(100.0 * n_cancelled / n_orders, 2)`

Return `segment`, `n_orders`, `n_cancelled`, `cancel_pct`, sorted by `segment` ascending (SQLite sorts NULL first).
exercises.starter:
SELECT c.segment, COUNT(*) AS n_orders
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
hints: `SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts rows meeting a condition inside a group.
Multiply by `100.0`, not `100`: integer / integer truncates in SQLite.
exercises.explanation: Conditional aggregation puts a CASE inside an aggregate to compute several filtered counts in one pass, the standard way to pivot statuses into columns. Do not filter `WHERE status = 'cancelled'`: you would lose the denominator. And `1 / 17` is 0 in integer arithmetic, so force a float with `100.0 *` or `CAST(... AS REAL)`.

review.code:
import sqlite3
c = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
print(c.execute('SELECT 2 / 3, 2.0 / 3').fetchone())
review.why: Integer division truncates; one float operand fixes it.

review.code:
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'cancelled' THEN 1 ____ 0 END) AS n_cancelled
FROM orders
review.why: ELSE 0 so non-cancelled rows add nothing.

review.q: Why not just add `WHERE status = 'cancelled'` to compute the rate?
options: It removes the other orders, so the denominator is wrong
review.why: The rate needs all orders in the denominator.

review.front: Shorter alternative to `SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` in SQLite/PostgreSQL?
review.back: `SUM(cond)` in SQLite (booleans are 0/1); `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE cond)` in PostgreSQL and SQLite.

exercises.title: A lazy batching generator
exercises.prompt:
Write a **generator** `batched(iterable, n)` that yields tuples of `n` consecutive items (the last tuple may be shorter). It must be lazy: it has to work on any iterable, including an infinite one like `itertools.count()`.

Example: `list(batched("abcde", 2))` returns `[("a", "b"), ("c", "d"), ("e",)]`.
exercises.starter:
def batched(iterable, n):
    pass
hints: Call `iter(iterable)` once so every slice continues where the last one stopped.
`tuple(itertools.islice(it, n))` takes up to n items; an empty tuple means you are done.
exercises.explanation: A function containing `yield` returns a generator that produces values on demand, so memory stays flat and infinite inputs are fine. Calling `iter()` once is the key: slicing the same iterator repeatedly consumes it chunk by chunk. Pitfall: `len()` or indexing does not work on generators; and a generator can only be consumed once.

review.code:
g = (x for x in range(3))
print(sum(g), sum(g))
review.why: A generator is exhausted after one pass.

review.code:
from itertools import accumulate
print(list(accumulate([1, 2, 3])))
review.why: accumulate yields running totals.

review.q: What does calling a function that contains `yield` return?
review.why: The body does not run until you iterate.
`yield from` delegates to a sub-iterator.

more.prompt:

hints: Call `iter(iterable)` once, before the loop.
`list(itertools.islice(it, n))` takes up to n items; an empty list means you are done.
more.explanation: Same as `batched`, with lists instead of tuples. `yield` hands out one group at a time, so memory stays small even on huge inputs.

more.prompt:

Example: `list(batched_sums([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2))` returns `[3, 7, 5]`.
hints: Same loop as `batched`: `chunk = list(islice(it, n))`, stop when it is empty.
Yield `sum(chunk)` instead of the chunk itself.
more.explanation: A generator can transform each batch before handing it out. This is how you aggregate a stream (minutes into 5-minute totals) without loading it all.

more.prompt:
A log file is read line by line. Write a **generator** `read_in_batches(lines, n)` that yields tuples of `n` consecutive lines (the last tuple may be shorter). It must be lazy and work on an infinite iterator too.

Example: `list(read_in_batches(["l1", "l2", "l3"], 2))` returns `[("l1", "l2"), ("l3",)]`.

**At work:** you send a huge log to a database 1,000 lines at a time.
hints: `it = iter(lines)` once, so each slice continues where the last one stopped.
`tuple(islice(it, n))`; return when it comes back empty.
more.explanation: Calling `iter()` once is the key: each `islice` takes the next n lines from the same iterator. A generator never holds the whole file in memory.

exercises.prompt:
Write `two_sum(nums, target)` returning a tuple `(i, j)` with `i < j` and `nums[i] + nums[j] == target`, in **one pass** (O(n)). If several pairs exist, return the one with the smallest `j` (and for that `j`, the smallest `i`). Return `None` if there is no pair. An element cannot be used twice.

Example: `two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9)` returns `(0, 1)`.
exercises.starter:
def two_sum(nums, target):
    pass
hints: For each `x`, the partner you need is `target - x`.
Store `value -> first index` in a dict; check for the partner **before** inserting `x`.
exercises.explanation: The dict trades memory for time: each lookup is O(1), so one pass is enough instead of the O(n^2) double loop. Checking before inserting is what prevents pairing an element with itself. Using `setdefault` keeps the first index of each value, which gives the smallest `i`.

review.front: Time and space complexity of hash-map two-sum?
review.back: O(n) time (one pass, O(1) lookups) and O(n) extra space for the dict.

review.q: Why check `target - x in seen` before adding x?
options: so x is not paired with itself
review.why: With target = 2x, inserting first would match x with itself.
setdefault only inserts when the key is missing.

review.code:
if target - x ____ seen:
    return (seen[target - x], j)
review.why: Membership on a dict tests keys in O(1).

hints: For each price `x`, the partner you need is `budget - x`.
Keep `price -> first index` in a dict; look for the partner **before** adding `x`.
more.explanation: The dict remembers what you have already seen, so each item needs one lookup instead of a second loop. Checking before inserting stops an item from pairing with itself.

exercises.title: Binary search: first index >= x
exercises.prompt:
`nums` is sorted ascending (it may contain duplicates). Write `lower_bound(nums, x)` returning the **first index** `i` with `nums[i] >= x`, or `len(nums)` if there is none. Implement the binary search yourself (O(log n)).

Example: `lower_bound([1, 3, 5, 7], 4)` returns `2`.
exercises.starter:
def lower_bound(nums, x):
    pass
hints: Search on the half-open range `[lo, hi)` with `lo, hi = 0, len(nums)`.
If `nums[mid] < x` the answer is right of mid (`lo = mid + 1`), otherwise mid may be it (`hi = mid`).
exercises.explanation: Binary search halves the candidate range each step, so a million items need about 20 comparisons. The half-open range `[lo, hi)` with `while lo < hi` and `hi = mid` avoids the classic off-by-one errors and infinite loops. In production, `bisect.bisect_left` does exactly this.

review.code:
import bisect
print(bisect.bisect_left([1, 2, 2, 3], 2), bisect.bisect_right([1, 2, 2, 3], 2))
review.why: bisect_left gives the first position of 2, bisect_right the position after the last.

review.q: Roughly how many steps does binary search need on 1,000,000 sorted items?
review.why: log2(1,000,000) is about 20.

review.code: mid = (lo + hi) ____ 2
review.why: Integer division gives a valid index.

review.front: What must be true of the input for binary search?
review.back: It must be sorted (more generally: the condition you test must be monotonic, all False then all True).

more.prompt:
`nums` is sorted ascending (it may contain duplicates). Write `upper_bound(nums, x)` returning the **first index** `i` with `nums[i] > x` (strictly greater), or `len(nums)` if there is none. Implement the binary search yourself.

Example: `upper_bound([1, 3, 5, 7], 5)` returns `3`.
hints: Same loop as `lower_bound`, with `lo, hi = 0, len(nums)`.
The only change: move right when `nums[mid] <= x` (not just `<`).
more.explanation: Changing `<` to `<=` moves the answer past every copy of `x`. `upper_bound - lower_bound` is how many times `x` appears; in production it is `bisect.bisect_right`.

**At work:** finding where a reporting period starts in a long sorted log.
hints: Half-open range: `lo, hi = 0, len(dates)` and `while lo < hi:`.
If `dates[mid] < day`, the answer is to the right (`lo = mid + 1`), else `hi = mid`.
more.explanation: Binary search works on anything that is sorted, numbers or text. ISO dates sort correctly as strings because the biggest unit (the year) comes first.

more.prompt:
`prices` is sorted ascending. Write `count_below(prices, x)` returning **how many** prices are strictly below `x`. Implement the binary search yourself (no loop over every price).

Example: `count_below([5, 10, 20], 15)` returns `2`.

**At work:** 'how many products are cheaper than the competitor's price?'

Use the `lower_bound` loop: `lo = mid + 1` when `prices[mid] < x`, else `hi = mid`.
more.explanation: In a sorted list, the position of the first value `>= x` equals the count of values below `x`. Binary search finds it in about 20 steps for a million prices.

exercises.title: Vectorized z-scores and outlier flags
exercises.prompt:
`numpy` is imported as `np`. Write two functions with **no Python loops**:

1. `standardize(X)`: for a 2D array (or nested list), return the column-wise z-scores `(X - mean) / std` using the population std (`ddof=0`). Columns with std 0 must give 0.
2. `flag_outliers(X, z)`: return a boolean array of the same shape, `True` where `|z-score| > z`.

Example: `standardize(np.array([[1, 10], [3, 10], [5, 10]]))` returns about `[[-1.2247, 0], [0, 0], [1.2247, 0]]`.
hints: `X.mean(axis=0)` has shape (n_cols,) and broadcasts against X of shape (n_rows, n_cols).
Avoid dividing by zero: replace 0 stds with 1 first, then use `np.where(sd == 0, 0.0, ...)`.
Comparisons on arrays return boolean arrays: `np.abs(Z) > z`.
exercises.explanation: Broadcasting stretches the (n_cols,) mean and std across every row, so the whole computation is one vectorized expression. `axis=0` means 'collapse the rows', i.e. one value per column. Pitfall: dividing by a zero std gives NaN and a warning; guard it with `np.where`. Note that pandas' `.std()` defaults to `ddof=1` while numpy uses `ddof=0`.

import numpy as np
print((np.ones((3, 1)) + np.ones(4)).shape)
review.why: (3,1) and (4,) broadcast to (3,4): size-1 dimensions stretch.

a[a < 0] = 0

review.why: A boolean mask selects (and can assign to) matching elements.

review.why: axis=0 collapses the rows, leaving one mean per column.
Use & (with parentheses) for element-wise AND; `and` fails on arrays.

exercises.title: The ML workflow
exercises.prompt:
A typical project runs: frame the business question, get and clean data, split it, build features, train, evaluate, then deploy and monitor.

- **Supervised** learning has a target `y` (regression for numbers, classification for classes); **unsupervised** learning finds structure without labels (clustering, dimensionality reduction).
- The **test set** is held out until the very end and estimates performance on unseen data; model and hyperparameter choices are made on training data (via a validation set or cross-validation).
- `stratify=y` keeps class proportions identical in train and test, which matters for small or imbalanced data.
- Always compare against a **baseline** (majority class, mean prediction): a 95% accuracy is meaningless if 95% of rows are one class.
- Every fitted transformation (scaler, imputer, encoder) is learned on the training data only, then applied to test.

questions.q: A retailer wants to group customers into segments without any predefined labels. Which kind of problem is this?
questions.why: There is no target to predict; the goal is to discover groups, which is clustering.

questions.q: Why should the test set not be used to choose hyperparameters?
options: It is too small to train on
Tuning on it makes the final score optimistically biased, so it no longer estimates unseen-data performance
scikit-learn raises an error if you do
questions.why: Every decision made by looking at the test set leaks information into the model; use validation data or CV instead.

questions.q: On a dataset with 3% fraud, a model reaches 97% accuracy. What is the first thing to check?
options: Whether a model predicting 'no fraud' always also gets 97%
Whether the learning rate is too high
Whether the test set is larger than the train set
questions.why: The majority-class baseline already scores 97%; accuracy hides that the model may detect no fraud at all.

questions.q: What does `train_test_split(X, y, stratify=y)` guarantee?
options: Train and test have (almost) the same class proportions as y
questions.why: Stratification preserves label proportions; reproducibility comes from `random_state`, not `stratify`.

questions.q: Predicting next month's revenue (in euros) per store is a...
questions.why: The target is a continuous number, so it is supervised regression.

exercises.explanation: Split first, then do every fitted step on the training part only, and keep the test set for one final, honest estimate. Always report a baseline next to your model. Pitfall: tuning on the test set and then quoting that score to a client.

review.front: Supervised vs unsupervised in one line?
review.back: Supervised learns a mapping X -> y from labeled data; unsupervised finds structure in X with no y.

review.code:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
X = list(range(10))
a, b = train_test_split(X, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
print(len(a), len(b))
review.why: 30% of 10 rows go to test.

review.q: Which argument makes a train/test split reproducible?
review.why: random_state fixes the shuffling seed.

exercises.title: LRU cache
exercises.prompt:
Write a class `LRUCache(capacity)` with two O(1) methods:

- `get(key)`: return the value, or `-1` if absent. A successful get marks the key as most recently used.
- `put(key, value)`: insert or update the key and mark it most recently used. If the cache exceeds `capacity`, evict the **least recently used** key.

Example with capacity 2: `put(1, 1)`, `put(2, 2)`, `get(1)` returns 1, `put(3, 3)` evicts key 2, so `get(2)` returns -1.
hints: `collections.OrderedDict` remembers order and has `move_to_end(key)` and `popitem(last=False)`, both O(1).
Keep the most recently used key at the end; evict from the front.
exercises.explanation: An LRU cache needs O(1) lookup (a hash map) and O(1) reordering (a linked list); OrderedDict is both. Every access moves the key to the end, so the front is always the least recently used. Pitfall: forgetting that `put` on an existing key must also refresh its position. For caching a pure function, use `functools.lru_cache`.

review.code:
from collections import OrderedDict
d = OrderedDict(a=1, b=2, c=3)
d.move_to_end('a')
print(list(d))
review.why: move_to_end sends the key to the end (most recent).

review.code: d.popitem(last=____)   # remove the OLDEST entry
review.why: last=False pops from the front.

review.q: Which decorator memoizes a pure function with LRU eviction?
review.why: lru_cache stores results keyed by the (hashable) arguments.

review.front: Which two structures make an LRU cache O(1)?
review.back: A hash map for lookup plus a doubly linked list for recency order (OrderedDict combines both).

more.prompt:
A shop shows each visitor their recently viewed products. Write a class `RecentlyViewed(capacity)` with two methods:

- `view(item)`: record that `item` was viewed. It becomes the most recent; viewing it again does not create a duplicate. If more than `capacity` items are stored, forget the **oldest** one.
- `items()`: return the stored items as a list, **most recent first**.

Example with capacity 3: view `a`, `b`, `c` gives `['c', 'b', 'a']`; then view `a` gives `['a', 'c', 'b']`; then view `d` gives `['d', 'a', 'c']`.
hints: `collections.OrderedDict` keeps order and has `move_to_end(key)` and `popitem(last=False)`.
Keep the most recent at the end; `list(reversed(self.data))` lists them newest first.
more.explanation: This is an LRU cache without values: every view moves the item to the end, so the front is always the oldest and is evicted first.

more.prompt:
A web app keeps a limited number of logged-in sessions in memory. Write a class `SessionStore(capacity)` with two O(1) methods:

- `get(token)`: return the user of that session, or `None` if absent. A successful get marks the token as most recently used.
- `put(token, user)`: insert or update the session and mark it most recently used. If there are more than `capacity` sessions, remove the **least recently used** one.

Example with capacity 2: `put('t1', 'ana')`, `put('t2', 'bo')`, `get('t1')` returns `'ana'`, `put('t3', 'cy')` removes `t2`, so `get('t2')` returns `None`.
hints: Use an `OrderedDict`: `move_to_end` on every access, `popitem(last=False)` to evict.
`put` on an existing token must also move it to the end.
more.explanation: Same structure as `LRUCache`, returning `None` instead of -1. The OrderedDict gives O(1) lookups and O(1) reordering.

more.prompt:
Prices fetched from a slow API are cached. Write a class `PriceCache(capacity)` with:

- `get(sku)`: return the price, or `-1` if absent. A successful get marks the sku as most recently used.
- `put(sku, price)`: insert or update and mark it most recently used. If the cache exceeds `capacity`, evict the **least recently used** sku.
- an attribute `evictions`: how many skus have been evicted so far (starts at 0).

Example with capacity 2: `put(1, 1)`, `put(2, 2)`, `get(1)` returns 1, `put(3, 3)` evicts sku 2 (`evictions` is now 1).

**At work:** the eviction count tells you if the cache is too small.
hints: Start with `self.evictions = 0` in `__init__`.
Add 1 to it each time you call `popitem(last=False)`.
more.explanation: An LRU cache plus a counter. Watching how often a cache evicts is how you choose its size in practice.

exercises.title: Linear regression essentials
exercises.prompt:
Linear regression models `y ≈ Xw + b` and, with OLS, picks the weights that minimize the **mean squared error** `MSE = mean((y - ŷ)²)`. The closed-form solution is `w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy` (with a column of ones for the intercept); in practice a least-squares solver is used for numerical stability.

- **Gradient descent** reaches the same optimum iteratively: `w ← w - lr · (2/n)·Xᵀ(Xw - y)`.
- **R² = 1 - SS_res / SS_tot** measures the share of variance explained versus predicting the mean; it is 0 for the mean predictor and can be negative on test data.
- **RMSE** is in the units of `y` and easier to explain to a client; **MAE** is more robust to outliers because errors are not squared.
- A coefficient is the expected change in `y` for a one-unit change in that feature, *holding the others fixed*; correlated features (multicollinearity) make individual coefficients unstable.

questions.q: A model has R² = -0.2 on the test set. What does this mean?
options: Impossible, R² is always between 0 and 1
It predicts worse than always predicting the mean of y
The features are negatively correlated with y
questions.why: R² < 0 means SS_res > SS_tot: the model is worse than the constant mean prediction.

questions.q: Why does MSE penalize outliers more than MAE?
options: It squares the errors, so large errors dominate
It is computed on the log scale
questions.why: An error of 10 contributes 100 to MSE but only 10 to MAE.

questions.q: Two features are almost perfectly correlated. What happens to OLS?
options: The individual coefficients become unstable with large variance, though predictions may still be fine
questions.why: XᵀX is near-singular, so the weight can be shared arbitrarily between the two features.

questions.q: In gradient descent for MSE, what happens if the learning rate is far too large?
options: It converges faster to the same solution
It finds a different global minimum
questions.why: Steps that are too big jump over the minimum and the loss can grow without bound.

questions.q: A client asks 'how wrong are your predictions, typically?'. Which metric is easiest to communicate?
questions.why: RMSE/MAE are in the target's units; MSE is in squared units and R² is relative.

exercises.explanation: OLS minimizes MSE and has a closed form; gradient descent gets there iteratively. R² compares the model to the mean predictor, and RMSE/MAE talk in business units. Pitfall: reading coefficients as causal effects, or as importance when features are on different scales.

review.code:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([1., 2., 3.])
p = np.array([1., 2., 5.])
print(round(float(np.mean((y - p) ** 2)), 3))
review.why: Errors 0, 0, -2 -> squared 0, 0, 4 -> mean 4/3.

review.front: R² formula?
review.back: 1 - SS_res/SS_tot = 1 - Σ(y-ŷ)² / Σ(y-ȳ)²

review.code:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([1., 2., 3.])
p = np.full(3, 2.)
print(1 - ((y - p) ** 2).sum() / ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum())
review.why: Predicting the mean gives R² = 0.

exercises.title: Logistic regression and classification metrics
exercises.prompt:
Logistic regression computes a linear score `z = Xw + b` and turns it into a probability with the **sigmoid** `σ(z) = 1/(1+e^-z)`; it is trained by minimizing **log-loss** (cross-entropy), and a coefficient is a change in **log-odds**.

- The default decision rule is `p ≥ 0.5`, but the threshold is a business choice.
- The **confusion matrix** counts TP, FP, FN, TN. In sklearn, `confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)` has **true labels in rows, predictions in columns**: `[[TN, FP], [FN, TP]]`.
- **Precision** = TP/(TP+FP): of the flagged cases, how many are right. **Recall** = TP/(TP+FN): of the real positives, how many we caught.
- **F1** is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so it is low if either is low.
- Choose by error cost: missed cancer (FN) is costly -> favor recall; a spam filter that hides real mail (FP) is costly -> favor precision.

questions.q: A fraud model flags 100 transactions; 80 are really fraud. There were 200 frauds in total. Precision and recall?
questions.why: Precision = 80/100; recall = 80/200.

questions.q: In `confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred)` for binary labels {0, 1}, where are the false negatives?
questions.why: Rows are true labels, columns predictions: true 1 predicted 0 is [1, 0].

questions.q: Raising the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.8 usually...
options: changes nothing since the model is the same
questions.why: Fewer, more confident positives: fewer FP (precision up) but more FN (recall down).

questions.q: Why F1 instead of the arithmetic mean of precision and recall?
options: The harmonic mean punishes a very low value in either one
questions.why: Precision 1.0 with recall 0.01 gives an arithmetic mean of ~0.5 but an F1 of ~0.02.

questions.q: A logistic regression coefficient of 0.7 on a feature means...
options: the probability rises by 0.7 per unit
the log-odds rise by 0.7 per unit (odds multiplied by e^0.7 ≈ 2)
questions.why: The model is linear in log-odds; exp(coef) is the odds ratio.

exercises.explanation: Logistic regression outputs probabilities; the threshold turns them into decisions, and precision/recall describe the two kinds of errors. Pitfall: reading sklearn's confusion matrix with predictions in rows; it is true labels in rows.

review.code:
tp, fp, fn = 8, 2, 4
print(round(tp / (tp + fp), 2), round(tp / (tp + fn), 2))
review.why: Precision 8/10, recall 8/12.

review.front: Layout of sklearn's binary confusion matrix?
review.back: [[TN, FP], [FN, TP]]: true labels in rows, predictions in columns.

review.q: Screening for a serious disease: which metric matters most?
review.why: Missing a sick patient (FN) is the costly error, so maximize recall.

exercises.title: Bias, variance and regularization
exercises.prompt:
Expected test error decomposes into **bias²** (error from a model too simple to capture the pattern), **variance** (sensitivity to the particular training sample) and irreducible noise.

- **Underfitting**: high train and high test error (high bias). **Overfitting**: low train error, much higher test error (high variance).
- More data mainly reduces variance; a more flexible model reduces bias but raises variance.
- **Ridge** (L2) adds `alpha·Σw²`: it shrinks all coefficients smoothly toward zero and handles correlated features well.
- **Lasso** (L1) adds `alpha·Σ|w|`: it can set coefficients exactly to zero, so it also selects features.
- **ElasticNet** mixes both. Larger `alpha` = stronger penalty = simpler model. Features must be **scaled** first, or the penalty hits features unevenly.

questions.q: Train R² = 0.99, test R² = 0.55. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.why: A big gap between train and test performance is the signature of variance.

questions.q: Both train and test errors are high and close to each other. Which action is most likely to help?
options: Use a more flexible model or add better features
Drop half the features at random
questions.why: That is underfitting (bias): more data or more regularization will not fix a model that is too simple.

questions.q: Why can Lasso produce exactly-zero coefficients while Ridge does not?
options: The L1 penalty has a corner at 0, so the optimum often lands on an axis
Lasso drops features with low variance first
questions.why: The |w| penalty is non-differentiable at 0, so the solution sticks there; the smooth w² penalty only shrinks.

questions.q: You have 30 highly correlated features. Which is usually the more stable choice?
options: Lasso, which arbitrarily keeps one per group
Ridge (or ElasticNet), which spreads weight across the group
questions.why: Lasso picks one correlated feature somewhat randomly; Ridge shares the weight and is more stable.

questions.q: What happens to a Ridge model as alpha goes to infinity?
options: All coefficients go to 0 and it predicts roughly the mean
questions.why: The penalty dominates and pushes every weight to zero (the intercept is not penalized).

questions.q: Why scale features before Ridge or Lasso?
options: Otherwise the penalty depends on the units: a feature in grams is penalized differently than in kilograms
questions.why: Coefficient size depends on feature scale, so an unscaled penalty is arbitrary.

exercises.explanation: Diagnose with the train/test gap: big gap = variance, both bad = bias. Regularization trades a little bias for less variance; L1 also selects features. Pitfall: tuning alpha without scaling, or comparing coefficient magnitudes across unscaled features.

review.front: Ridge vs Lasso penalty?
review.back: Ridge: alpha·Σw² (shrinks). Lasso: alpha·Σ|w| (shrinks and zeroes out, selects).

review.code:
import numpy as np
w = np.array([3., -4.])
print(np.abs(w).sum(), (w ** 2).sum())
review.why: L1 norm 3 + 4, squared L2 norm 9 + 16.

review.q: Low train error, high test error. Which helps?
review.why: Overfitting is variance; regularization reduces it.

exercises.prompt:

hints: Sort by start time and keep the end times of rooms in use.
A min-heap (`heapq`) gives the earliest-ending room in O(1); reuse it if it ends by the new start.
The heap size at the end is the answer.
exercises.explanation: After sorting by start, only the room that frees up first matters, which is exactly what a min-heap gives in O(log n). Overall O(n log n). exercises.title: Cross-validation
exercises.prompt:
A single train/validation split gives a noisy estimate. **K-fold cross-validation** splits the training data into K folds, trains K times on K-1 folds and validates on the remaining one, then averages the K scores; the **standard deviation** tells you how stable the estimate is.

- **StratifiedKFold** keeps class proportions in every fold; sklearn uses it by default for classifiers when you pass `cv=5`.
- `KFold` does **not shuffle** by default; if the rows are sorted (by class or date), set `shuffle=True` with a `random_state`.
- **GroupKFold** keeps all rows of one entity (customer, patient) in the same fold, to avoid leakage across related rows.
- Time series need **TimeSeriesSplit** (train on the past, validate on the future), not shuffled folds.
- CV is for model selection; the final model is then refit on all training data, and the test set is still used only once.

questions.q: Your dataset has several rows per patient. Which splitter avoids leakage?
questions.why: Rows of the same patient are correlated; they must all be in train or all in validation.

questions.q: The CSV is sorted by class (all 0s then all 1s). You use `KFold(5)` without shuffle on a classifier. What happens?
options: Some folds contain almost only one class, giving misleading scores
questions.why: KFold takes contiguous blocks by default; use StratifiedKFold or shuffle=True.

questions.q: 5-fold CV gives scores 0.81, 0.83, 0.80, 0.82, 0.62. What should you conclude?
options: The mean ~0.78 hides instability; investigate the outlier fold
questions.why: High variance across folds signals unstable performance or a special subgroup; report mean and std.

questions.q: After choosing a model with 5-fold CV, what is the usual next step?
options: Keep one of the 5 fold models
Refit the chosen configuration on the full training set, then evaluate once on test
Re-run CV on the test set
questions.why: CV estimates performance of a configuration; the deployed model uses all training data.

questions.q: Compared with 5-fold, 10-fold CV...
options: trains on more data per fold and costs twice as many fits
questions.why: Each fold trains on 90% instead of 80%, at the price of 10 fits instead of 5.

exercises.explanation: CV turns one noisy estimate into K, and the spread matters as much as the mean. Match the splitter to the data's structure: stratified for classes, group for entities, time-series for time. Pitfall: KFold without shuffling on sorted data.

review.code:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
print([len(te) for _, te in KFold(3).split(np.arange(10))])
review.why: 10 rows into 3 folds: the first fold gets the extra row.

review.q: Which splitter for multiple rows per customer?
review.why: GroupKFold keeps each group in a single fold.

review.front: What does `cv=5` mean for a classifier in cross_val_score?
review.back: StratifiedKFold(5), no shuffle.

exercises.prompt:

exercises.prompt:

exercises.title: Trees and random forests
exercises.prompt:
A **decision tree** splits the data greedily on the feature/threshold that most reduces impurity (Gini or entropy for classification, MSE for regression). Trees need no scaling, capture interactions and non-linearities, but a deep tree **overfits** (high variance); `max_depth`, `min_samples_leaf` control it.

- A **random forest** averages many deep trees, each trained on a **bootstrap sample** (bagging) and considering a random subset of features at each split (`max_features`); decorrelating the trees is what reduces variance.
- Rows left out of a tree's bootstrap give a free **out-of-bag** (OOB) estimate.
- `feature_importances_` (mean decrease in impurity) is computed on training data and is **biased toward high-cardinality / continuous features**; permutation importance on held-out data is more reliable.
- Adding more trees does not cause overfitting; it only stabilizes the average at a cost in time.

questions.q: Why does a random forest choose a random subset of features at each split?
options: To decorrelate the trees, so averaging reduces variance more
questions.why: If one feature dominates, all bagged trees look alike; feature subsampling makes their errors less correlated.

questions.q: Does a decision tree need feature scaling?
options: No, splits depend only on the order of values within a feature
questions.why: A threshold split is invariant to monotonic transformations of a feature.

questions.q: An ID-like column with many unique values gets the highest `feature_importances_`. Most likely reason?
options: It is truly the most predictive
Impurity-based importance is biased toward high-cardinality features that allow many splits
The forest has too few trees
questions.why: Many possible thresholds let the tree memorize; check with permutation importance on validation data.

questions.q: Going from 100 to 1000 trees in a random forest will most likely...
questions.why: More trees reduce the variance of the average; performance plateaus but does not degrade.

questions.q: What is the out-of-bag score?
options: Validation score using, for each row, only trees that did not see it in their bootstrap
questions.why: About 37% of rows are left out of each bootstrap, giving a built-in validation estimate.

exercises.explanation: Single trees are interpretable but high-variance; forests reduce variance by averaging decorrelated trees. Pitfall: presenting impurity-based importances to a client as truth; they are biased and computed on training data.

p = [0.5, 0.5]
print(1 - sum(x * x for x in p))
review.why: Gini = 1 - Σp² = 1 - 0.5 = 0.5, the max for two classes.

review.front: Bagging in one sentence?
review.back: Train many models on bootstrap samples and average them to reduce variance.

review.q: Which hyperparameter limits a tree's overfitting most directly?
review.why: Depth caps model complexity.

exercises.title: Gradient boosting, XGBoost, LightGBM
exercises.prompt:
**Boosting** builds trees **sequentially**: each new shallow tree is fit to the **negative gradient** of the loss for the current predictions (for squared error that is simply the residuals), and is added with a shrinkage factor, the **learning rate**.

- Bagging (random forest) mainly reduces variance; boosting mainly reduces bias, and **can overfit** if you add too many trees.
- `learning_rate` and `n_estimators` trade off: a smaller learning rate needs more trees but usually generalizes better. **Early stopping** on a validation set picks the number of trees.
- **XGBoost** adds regularization on leaf weights (lambda, gamma) and second-order gradients; **LightGBM** grows trees leaf-wise with histogram binning, making it very fast on large data (watch `num_leaves`). sklearn's `HistGradientBoosting*` is similar.
- Other useful knobs: `max_depth` (3-8 typical), `subsample` (row sampling, 'stochastic' boosting), column sampling.
- On tabular data, tuned gradient boosting is usually the strongest baseline.

questions.q: For squared-error loss, each new tree in gradient boosting is fit to...
questions.why: The negative gradient of ½(y - F)² w.r.t. F is y - F, the residual.

questions.q: Main difference between bagging and boosting?
options: Bagging trains trees in parallel on bootstraps; boosting trains trees sequentially, each correcting the previous ones
questions.why: Independence (bagging) vs sequential error correction (boosting).

questions.q: You halve the learning rate. To keep similar performance you typically...
questions.why: Each tree contributes less, so more trees are needed; early stopping finds the right count.

questions.q: Validation loss of a boosting model starts rising after 300 trees while training loss keeps falling. What should you do?
options: Use early stopping around 300 trees (or lower the learning rate)
questions.why: Unlike random forests, boosting overfits as trees are added.

questions.q: What makes LightGBM fast on large datasets?
options: Histogram-based binning of features and leaf-wise tree growth
questions.why: Binning reduces split candidates; leaf-wise growth reduces loss quickly (but can overfit; constrain num_leaves).

exercises.explanation: Boosting = sequential small trees fit to gradients, shrunk by the learning rate. Tune learning rate, number of trees (with early stopping) and depth together. Pitfall: assuming more trees is always safe, as with a random forest.

lr = 0.1
r = [2, -1]
print([f0 + lr * x for x in r])
review.why: Each prediction moves a fraction lr of the residual-fitting tree's output.

review.q: Which can overfit when you add many more estimators?
review.why: Boosting keeps fitting the training residuals; forests just average.

review.front: What is early stopping in boosting?
review.back: Stop adding trees when the validation score stops improving for N rounds.

exercises.title: Feature engineering and pipelines
exercises.prompt:
**Scaling** matters for distance- and gradient-based models (k-NN, SVM, k-means, PCA, regularized linear models) but not for trees. `StandardScaler` gives mean 0 / std 1; `MinMaxScaler` maps to [0, 1] and is sensitive to outliers; `RobustScaler` uses median and IQR.

- Categorical features: **one-hot** for nominal categories (`OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown='ignore')` to survive unseen values); ordinal encoding only when there is a real order or for tree models; target encoding for very high cardinality, but it must be fit inside CV to avoid leakage.
- `ColumnTransformer` applies different preprocessing to different columns; `Pipeline` chains preprocessing and the model into one estimator.
- A pipeline guarantees that `fit` learns scalers/imputers/encoders on training folds only, and the same transformations are reused at predict time: no leakage, no train/serve skew.
- Step parameters are addressed as `step__param` (e.g. `clf__C`) in grid searches.
- Useful engineered features often come from domain knowledge: ratios, dates (day of week, seasonality), aggregates per entity, log of skewed amounts.

questions.q: Which model does NOT need feature scaling?
questions.why: Tree splits are invariant to monotonic rescaling; the others rely on distances or penalties.

questions.q: Why put the scaler inside a Pipeline instead of scaling X before cross-validation?
options: So the scaler is fit on each training fold only, preventing leakage of validation statistics
questions.why: Scaling all of X first uses validation/test means and stds during training.

questions.q: Production data contains a city never seen in training. With `OneHotEncoder()` defaults, what happens at transform time?
options: It is encoded as all zeros
It raises an error; use handle_unknown='ignore'
It is mapped to the most frequent city
questions.why: The default handle_unknown='error' raises; 'ignore' encodes unknowns as an all-zero row.

questions.q: A 'zip code' column has 30,000 levels. Which approach is most reasonable?
options: Ordinal encode 1..30000 for a linear model
Target/frequency encoding fit inside CV, or group into coarser regions
questions.why: One-hot explodes dimensionality; ordinal codes imply a fake order for linear models; target encoding must be fit on training folds only.

questions.q: In a Pipeline with steps `('prep', ...)` and `('clf', LogisticRegression())`, how do you tune C in GridSearchCV?
questions.why: Nested parameters use the step name, two underscores, then the parameter.

exercises.explanation: Scale for distance/penalty-based models, one-hot nominal categories, and wrap everything in a Pipeline so preprocessing is learned on training data only. Pitfall: `fit_transform` on the full dataset before splitting.

exercises.title: Imbalanced data and threshold choice
exercises.prompt:
With rare positives (fraud, churn, defects), accuracy is misleading. Use threshold-free ranking metrics plus a deliberate threshold.

- **ROC-AUC** plots TPR vs FPR; it is the probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative, and 0.5 is random. Because FPR divides by the (huge) number of negatives, ROC-AUC can look excellent even when precision is poor.
- **PR-AUC** (average precision) plots precision vs recall; its random baseline equals the **positive rate**, so it is more informative when positives are rare.
- The **threshold** should be chosen from business costs (cost of FP vs FN, capacity of the team reviewing alerts) on validation data, not left at 0.5.
- `class_weight='balanced'` reweights the loss so errors on the rare class count more; it shifts predicted probabilities (they are no longer calibrated).
- Resampling (undersampling, SMOTE) is an alternative; it must be applied **only to training folds**, never to validation or test data.
- Use stratified splits so every fold contains positives.

questions.q: Positives are 1% of the data. A model has ROC-AUC 0.95 and PR-AUC 0.15. How do you read this?
options: It ranks well overall, but among flagged cases precision is still low; PR-AUC baseline is 0.01, so it is 15x better than random
The metrics are inconsistent, there is a bug
questions.why: Both are valid; PR-AUC exposes the low precision that the huge number of negatives hides in ROC.

questions.q: What is the PR-AUC of a random classifier when 5% of rows are positive?
questions.why: Random precision equals the prevalence at every recall level.

questions.q: The fraud team can review 200 alerts per day. How should the threshold be set?
options: Pick the threshold that flags about 200 transactions per day on validation data, then check precision/recall there
Use the threshold that maximizes ROC-AUC
questions.why: Thresholds are a business decision; ROC-AUC does not depend on the threshold at all.

questions.q: What does `class_weight='balanced'` change?
options: It weights each class inversely to its frequency in the loss, raising recall on the rare class
questions.why: Errors on the rare class cost more, which moves the decision boundary; probabilities become less calibrated.

questions.q: You oversample with SMOTE on the full dataset, then run cross-validation. What is wrong?
options: Synthetic points derived from validation rows leak into training, inflating scores
CV must be done before scaling
questions.why: Resampling belongs inside the pipeline (e.g. imblearn Pipeline) so it runs on training folds only.

exercises.explanation: Report PR-AUC (with its prevalence baseline) next to ROC-AUC, and set the threshold from costs or capacity on validation data. Pitfall: resampling before splitting, which leaks and inflates every metric.

exercises.title: Clustering with k-means
exercises.prompt:
**k-means** alternates two steps until assignments stop changing: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its points. It minimizes **inertia** (within-cluster sum of squared distances) and only finds a local optimum, so it is restarted several times (`n_init`) with k-means++ initialization.

- It assumes roughly spherical, similar-size clusters and uses Euclidean distance, so **scale features** first.
- Inertia always decreases as k grows; the **elbow** method looks for where the decrease flattens.
- The **silhouette** score `(b - a)/max(a, b)` (a = mean distance to own cluster, b = to the nearest other cluster) ranges from -1 to 1; higher is better and it can be compared across k.
- **DBSCAN** finds arbitrary shapes and labels outliers as noise without choosing k; hierarchical clustering gives a dendrogram.
- In consulting, clusters must be **profiled and named** (means per cluster) to be actionable segments.

questions.q: Why can't you choose k by minimizing inertia?
options: Inertia is not defined for k > 10
Inertia always decreases as k increases, reaching 0 when k = n
questions.why: More centroids always fit the points at least as well; look for an elbow or use silhouette.

questions.q: Customer features: age (years) and annual spend (euros). What must happen before k-means?
options: Scale the features, otherwise spend dominates the Euclidean distance
questions.why: Distances are dominated by the feature with the largest range.

questions.q: Data has two interleaved crescent-shaped groups. Which method is more appropriate than k-means?
questions.why: k-means assumes convex, spherical clusters; density-based DBSCAN follows arbitrary shapes.

questions.q: A point has silhouette close to -1. What does it mean?
options: It is closer on average to another cluster than to its own, probably misassigned
questions.why: s ≈ -1 means a > b: the neighboring cluster fits it better.

questions.q: Why does sklearn run k-means several times (`n_init`)?
options: Because results depend on initialization and it converges to local optima; the run with the lowest inertia is kept
questions.why: Different starts can end in different local minima.

exercises.explanation: k-means = assign to nearest centroid, recompute means, repeat. Scale first, compare k with silhouette (and an elbow plot), and profile clusters so the business can name them. Pitfall: unscaled features, where one large-range variable decides the whole segmentation.

review.q: Range of the silhouette score?
review.why: From -1 (misassigned) to 1 (dense, well separated).

exercises.title: PCA and dimensionality reduction
exercises.prompt:
**PCA** finds orthogonal directions (principal components) of maximal variance; the first component captures the most variance, the second the most of what remains, and so on. Mathematically they are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix, computed in practice by an SVD of the **centered** data.

- `explained_variance_ratio_` tells how much variance each component keeps; a common rule keeps enough components for 90-95% of the variance.
- PCA is scale sensitive: **standardize** first when features have different units.
- Components are linear combinations of all features, so they are harder to explain than original features; `components_` holds the loadings.
- Uses: compress correlated features, denoise, speed up models, and 2-D visualization. PCA is unsupervised, so the kept directions are not necessarily the most predictive.
- **t-SNE / UMAP** are non-linear and good for visualization, but distances between clusters in their plots are not meaningful and they are not used as a general preprocessing step.

questions.q: Why standardize before PCA when features are in different units?
options: Otherwise the feature with the largest variance (often just the largest unit) dominates the first component
questions.why: PCA maximizes variance, and variance depends on units.

questions.q: The first 3 components explain 60%, 25% and 10% of variance. How many to keep for at least 90%?
questions.why: Cumulative: 60%, 85%, 95%; three are needed to pass 90%.

questions.q: A client wants to know which original variables drive the prediction. Is PCA preprocessing helpful here?
options: Yes, components are easier to explain
Not really: each component mixes all features, which hurts interpretability
Yes, PCA selects the original features
questions.why: PCA trades interpretability for compression; feature selection keeps original variables.

questions.q: Which is true about principal components?
options: They are ordered by predictive power for y
They always have the same variance
questions.why: Components are orthogonal and ordered by explained variance, not by relevance to y.

questions.q: In a t-SNE plot, two clusters are far apart. What can you conclude?
options: They are far apart in the original space by the same ratio
Little about the true distance; t-SNE preserves local neighborhoods, not global distances
questions.why: t-SNE distorts global geometry; interpret only local groupings.

exercises.explanation: PCA = SVD of centered (usually standardized) data; keep components by cumulative explained variance. Pitfall: fitting PCA on the full dataset before the split, or forgetting that components are not interpretable features.

review.why: Cumulative explained-variance ratios.

review.q: Which PCA attribute holds the variance share per component?
review.why: It sums to 1 when all components are kept.

review.front: What does `PCA(n_components=0.95)` do?
review.back: Keeps the smallest number of components that explain at least 95% of the variance.

exercises.title: Hyperparameter tuning
exercises.prompt:
**Parameters** are learned by `fit` (coefficients, splits); **hyperparameters** are set before (C, max_depth, learning_rate) and chosen by validation.

- `GridSearchCV` tries every combination: cost multiplies with each added parameter. `RandomizedSearchCV` samples `n_iter` combinations from distributions, which explores more values of the parameters that matter for the same budget. Bayesian tools (Optuna) adapt where they sample.
- Search on a log scale for scale-type parameters (C, alpha, learning_rate): 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1...
- `best_score_` is the mean CV score of the winner; it is **optimistically biased** because it was selected as the maximum of many noisy estimates.
- **Nested CV** wraps the whole search in an outer CV loop to get an unbiased estimate of the *tuning procedure*; the final model is still a search refit on all data.
- With `refit=True` (default), the best configuration is refit on the whole training set and available as `best_estimator_`.
- If the best value sits on the edge of the grid, extend the grid.

questions.q: A grid with 4 values of C, 3 kernels and 5 gammas, evaluated with 5-fold CV, needs how many fits (excluding the refit)?
questions.why: 4 × 3 × 5 = 60 combinations, × 5 folds = 300 fits.

questions.q: Why can RandomizedSearchCV beat a grid with the same budget?
options: When only a few hyperparameters matter, random sampling tries many more distinct values of those
It always finds the global optimum
questions.why: A 3×3 grid tests only 3 values per parameter; 9 random draws test 9.

questions.q: Why is `best_score_` an optimistic estimate of future performance?
options: It is computed on training folds
It is the maximum over many configurations, so it benefits from selection noise
questions.why: Picking the best of many noisy scores biases upward; nested CV or a held-out test set corrects this.

questions.q: The best C found is 100, the largest value in your grid. What next?
options: Extend the grid to larger values, the optimum may lie beyond
questions.why: An optimum on the border means the search space was too narrow.

questions.q: What does nested CV estimate?
options: The generalization performance of the whole 'tune-then-fit' procedure
questions.why: The inner loop tunes; the outer loop scores the tuned model on data never used for tuning.

exercises.explanation: Tune on CV, search scale parameters on a log grid, prefer randomized search when there are many parameters, and report a score that was not used for selection. Pitfall: quoting `best_score_` as the expected production score.

review.back: Parameters are learned by fit (weights, splits); hyperparameters are set beforehand and tuned by validation (C, max_depth).

exercises.title: Leakage, regression metrics, time series
exercises.prompt:
**Data leakage** is when information unavailable at prediction time sneaks into training, producing great offline scores that collapse in production.

- **Target leakage**: a feature computed from or after the target (e.g. 'refund issued' to predict fraud, 'days in hospital' to predict admission).
- **Train-test contamination**: scaling, imputing, feature selection or resampling fit on the full dataset before splitting; fix it with Pipelines inside CV.
- **Time leakage**: random splits on temporal data let the model learn from the future. Use `TimeSeriesSplit` (expanding window: train on the past, test on the next block), and compute lag/rolling features only from past values.
- Regression metrics: **MAE** (robust, in units), **RMSE** (punishes large errors), **MAPE** (relative, explodes near 0), **R²** (vs mean baseline). Choose the one matching the business cost.
- A suspiciously high score (e.g. 0.99 AUC on a hard problem) is a leakage red flag: inspect the top features.

questions.q: Predicting loan default, the most important feature is 'number of collection calls'. What is the likely issue?
options: Target leakage: collection calls happen after (because of) the default
questions.why: That information is not available when the loan decision is made.

questions.q: You select the 20 best features using all the data, then run 5-fold CV and get 0.86 accuracy on pure noise. Why?
options: Feature selection saw the validation folds, so the chosen features fit their noise
questions.why: Selection must run inside each training fold (put it in a Pipeline).

questions.q: Forecasting daily sales, which validation is right?
options: TimeSeriesSplit: train on earlier days, validate on later ones
questions.why: The model must never see the future it is evaluated on.

questions.q: Sales are sometimes 0. Why avoid MAPE?
options: Dividing by actual values near 0 makes it explode or undefined
It punishes large errors too much
questions.why: Prefer MAE/RMSE or a weighted variant (WAPE).

questions.q: Errors are costly in proportion to their size, and occasional big misses are acceptable. Which metric fits best?
questions.why: MAE weighs errors linearly; RMSE would let rare large misses dominate.

exercises.explanation: Ask of every feature: would I know this at prediction time? Keep every fitted step inside the CV pipeline and split by time when time matters. Pitfall: an amazing first score; it is more often leakage than genius.

    print(len(tr), len(te))
review.why: Expanding window: test blocks of 8 // 4 = 2, training grows each split.

review.front: The leakage question to ask about each feature?
review.back: Would this value be known at the moment the prediction is made?

review.q: Which metric is in the target's units and robust to outliers?
review.why: MAE averages absolute errors.
